jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e106.summary: Rubric heading for Question 1, stating the question to be treated—whether God is in all things—and cross-referencing the parallel treatment in Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q.8, a.1.
concepts: cross-reference to Aquinas ST I q.8 a.1

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e115.summary: First objection against divine omnipresence: among causes, only intrinsic causes (matter and form) constitute a thing and are properly 'in' it, whereas God relates to creatures only as final or efficient (extrinsic) cause; therefore God is not in things but rather outside them.
claims: Only intrinsic causes (matter and form) are properly said to be 'in' the thing they constitute
God relates to creatures only as final or efficient (extrinsic) cause, not as matter or form
Therefore God is not in things but outside them

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e139.summary: Second objection against divine omnipresence: acting only on what is present is characteristic of limited power (as when acting through an intermediary supposit); since God's power is unlimited, he acts not only on the present but on the distant, and so is not in all things but distant from some.
claims: Acting only on what is present is a mark of limited causal power
God's power is unlimited
Therefore God acts on distant things and is not present in/to all things

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e153.summary: Sed contra: cites Scripture's affirmation that God fills heaven and earth, noting that this reading is upheld by the patristic authorities Augustine, Hilary, Ambrose, and Gregory in the gloss, thereby countering the two preceding objections.
claims: Scripture asserts that God fills heaven and earth
This scriptural reading is corroborated by patristic authority (Augustine, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory)

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e164.summary: Opens the responsio by dividing the inquiry into two articles: first, whether God is in all things; second, the mode of his being in them.
claims: The response requires treating, first, whether God is in all things, and second, the mode of his presence in them

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e175.summary: Article 1's main proof that God is in all things: a singular, immediate, actually-operating cause is simultaneous with its effect (per Physics II); God is such a cause with respect to every existing thing, hence is simultaneous with it. The minor is proved by distinguishing efficient-but-not-conserving causes (a builder to a house) from efficient-and-conserving causes (the sun to light in air): God, though not the immediate cause of every thing's production, is the immediate cause of its conservation, and per John 5:17 is always actually operating as long as the thing exists—otherwise things would lapse into nothing. Hence God is simultaneous with all things as long as they exist.
claims: A singular, immediate, actually-operating cause is simultaneous with its effect
God is the immediate conserving cause of every existing thing and operates continually as long as it exists
Therefore God is simultaneous with (present to) every existing thing

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e230.summary: First objection against the article's proof: even granting the whole argument, it does not establish the intended conclusion, since it only shows that God and creature are simultaneous. Simultaneity of duration (as Aristotle intends it) does not entail that one thing is 'in' another—Paris and Rome are simultaneous in duration without Paris being in Rome. Simultaneity of place likewise does not entail 'in-ness' without contact, and contact is impossible for an incorporeal agent.
claims: Simultaneity of duration between cause and effect does not entail that one is 'in' the other
Simultaneity of place does not entail 'in-ness' without contact, and an incorporeal agent cannot have contact
Therefore the article's proof fails to establish that God is in things

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e263.summary: Second objection against the article's proof: it is not even true that God is the immediate conserving cause of everything in things, since, for example, light in air is conserved by God only through the mediation of the sun, and likewise in many other cases; so at least in such cases the argument fails to conclude that God is in them.
claims: God is not the immediate conserving cause of everything; some things (e.g., light in air) are conserved through a mediating cause (the sun)
In such mediated cases the article's argument does not establish that God is in the thing

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e276.summary: Reply to the first counter-objection: saying God is 'in' things does not mean he is present as an intrinsic constituent part, but that he is present to the thing not merely by duration nor by bodily contact (since he is neither a body nor a power in a body) but by 'order' (ordo), which functions among spirits as position (situs) functions among bodies. This mode of presence is more excellent than positional presence, since it applies immediately to every part of the thing at once rather than only to an extremity as contact does; hence God can properly be said to be in things, not merely beside them.
claims: God's presence 'in' things is not presence as an intrinsic part but presence by 'order' (ordo), the spiritual analogue of bodily position (situs)
This ordo-presence reaches every part of the thing simultaneously, unlike contact which reaches only an extremity
Hence God can properly be said to be in things, not merely beside them
concepts: presence to the whole versus presence to an extremity

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e310.summary: Reply to the second counter-objection: even granting God is not the immediate conserving cause of everything found in things, the conclusion still stands. First, because God could, without any change in himself, immediately conserve if he willed, and the act of conserving does not itself cause presence but rather presupposes and indicates it a posteriori. Second, in every subsisting thing there is something immediately conserved by God: incorporeal things are wholly conserved by God directly, and corporeal things at least as to their matter—and since matter pervades the whole thing and nothing in the thing is without matter present to it, God, being immediately present to matter, is thereby present to everything in the thing, even where he does not immediately conserve it otherwise.
claims: God's mere potential (rather than actual) immediate conservation suffices to secure his presence
Conservation presupposes presence rather than causing it
Every subsisting thing has some element—matter in corporeal things, the whole in incorporeal things—that God conserves immediately, which secures his presence throughout the thing

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e354.summary: Opens Article 2 on the mode of God's presence in things, distinguishing one general and two special modes. The general mode holds that God is in things by essence, presence, and power. The modes of presence and power are well and consistently explained: God is in things because he is their cause, just as things are said to be 'in God' because created by him; corresponding to the two conditions of divine causality (intellect and free will), God is said to be present in things by presence in virtue of his intellectuality (things are 'present' to his view) and by power in virtue of his freedom (he can conserve or annihilate at will). How God is in things 'by essence,' however, is not so consistently explained among authors.
claims: There is one general mode and two special modes by which God is said to be in things
The general mode holds that God is in things by essence, presence, and power
God is in things by presence in virtue of his intellect, and by power in virtue of his free will
The mode of God's presence 'by essence' lacks a consistent account among authors

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e393.summary: Reports an opinion holding that God's existence in things is proportionally analogous to the existence of things in God: just as a thing considered under the being proper to its own genus is said to be in God's knowledge or power (not in the divine essence, since so considered it is not identical with God but merely the object terminating the divine operation), while considered under the virtual being of its cause it is said to be in the divine essence, being identical with it (per Anselm's dictum that the creature in God is the creating essence)—so, correspondingly, God considered in himself is not in any thing by essence but is above things, exceeding them in excellence, just as created nature is not in the divine essence but under it; whereas God considered under a being that is his causally rather than formally—namely the formal being of the creature—is in things by essence, not because the divine essence itself is in the thing, but because the essence that is formally the thing's is causally God's essence; thus just as the creature in God is the creating essence, so God in the creature is nothing other than the creature.
claims: The existence of things in God and God's existence in things are held to be proportionally analogous
A creature is 'in God' by essence only insofar as it is considered under its virtual/causal being, identical with the divine essence (per Anselm)
Correspondingly, God is 'in' a creature by essence in a causal sense: the creature's formal essence just is, causally, the divine essence
concepts: Anselm's dictum on creature and creator

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e443.summary: Critiques the opinion just reported, along with the common account of presence and power, as inadequate. The common account is faulty because God's intellect equally has in view things that exist and things not yet existing, and his freedom equally extends to producing or not producing, conserving or not conserving; so if presence and power were explained solely by intellect and will as described, God would be equally 'in' non-existent things as in existing ones, which is false. The essence-account just given is likewise insufficient because, as already proved in Article 1, God is in things not merely according to his effect but according to a real exhibition and presence of his essence—so more must be said than either prior account offers.
claims: The common presence/power account, grounded merely in intellect and will, wrongly implies God is equally 'in' non-existent things as in existing ones
The essence-account as causal identity of formal being is insufficient, since God's presence in things (per Article 1) is a real presential exhibition of essence, not merely a matter of effect
Both prior accounts therefore require correction

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e482.summary: Proposes the author's own solution. Since God's existence in things requires the existence of the things themselves (nothing can exist 'in' what is not), and things exist only through God's actual operation of creating and conserving them, the three general modes are drawn from the three things that concur on God's side toward production or conservation: the operation/action, the power from which the action proceeds, and the essence in which the power resides. Because the act of creation makes the thing exist and the act of conservation continues its existence, and existence makes the thing present to God and God present to it (God is made present to a thing only because the thing is made present to him), God is said to be in things by presence by reason of the producing and conserving action. Because this presence is not merely cognitional, as others hold, but a real exhibition—just as a seal's figure is neither made nor preserved in wax except by the real coexistence of the seal, so no thing is preserved in being except by the real coexistence of God—God is said to be in things by essence, on account of the real coexistence of the divine essence with things. Further, since action proceeds from essence only through power, God is said to be in things by power. These are the general modes according to natural being; beyond them, modes proper to spiritual being (the being of grace) apply as well—the hypostatic union, by which Christ's assumed humanity was reparative through congruity rather than necessity, so that God is in the assumed humanity by the grace of union, and the grace of adoption, by which God is in the person reparated as such, as was already discussed above at Distinction 14.
claims: God's existence in things presupposes the things' own existence, which itself depends on God's creative and conserving action
The three general modes (essence, presence, power) derive respectively from the essence, action, and power that concur in producing and conserving a thing
God's presence in things is a real exhibition of essence, not merely cognitional presence, illustrated by the seal-in-wax analogy
Beyond the natural modes, God is present in creatures by two further modes proper to grace: the hypostatic union (in Christ) and the grace of adoption (in the justified)

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e567.summary: Reply to the first opening objection (d1e115): God is not said to be in things as an intrinsic constituent part—indeed he is outside things—but is said to be in them by the immediate presence he has to any thing, reaching not merely an extremity as contact does, but every part of the thing, a presence effected by order rather than position, as explained above.
claims: The first objection wrongly equates 'being in' with 'being an intrinsic constituent part'
God's being in things is instead immediate presence to every part of the thing, effected by order rather than spatial contact

jsnvu6-d1e1804-d1e586.summary: Reply to the second opening objection (d1e139): making a thing present that previously did not exist at all, or conserving what has already been made, does not indicate imperfection or limitation of power but rather perfection, since without God's presence nothing else could exist or endure. By contrast, acting through some intermediary supposit does indicate imperfection, since it shows the causal power does not extend to everything and so necessarily presupposes something else; hence the two cases are not analogous.
claims: Producing and conserving all things directly is a mark of perfection, not limitation, since nothing else could exist or persist without it
Acting through an intermediary supposit indicates imperfection, since it shows the power does not extend to everything
The objection's analogy between the two cases therefore fails

jsnvu6-d1e1804.summary: Question 1 asks whether God is in all things and, if so, in what mode. Two objections deny divine omnipresence—one from the extrinsic character of final/efficient causality, one from the notion that unlimited power entails acting at a distance—and a sed contra invokes Scripture and patristic authority for omnipresence. The responsio divides into two articles. Article 1 argues that God is present to every existing thing because he is its immediate, continually-operating conserving cause, then answers two counter-objections by clarifying that divine 'in-ness' is constituted by order (ordo) rather than contact, and that presence is secured universally through matter even where immediate conservation of other elements is lacking. Article 2 examines the mode of that presence: it reports and then rejects an opinion that models God's presence in things on cognition/will or on the causal identity of essence, and proposes instead that God is in things by essence, presence, and power because of the real (not merely cognitive) coexistence required for creation and conservation, illustrated by the seal-in-wax analogy, adding further modes proper to grace (hypostatic union and adoption). The question closes by resolving the two opening objections in light of this account.
claims: God is present in all creatures as their immediate, continually-operating conserving cause, not merely as an extrinsic efficient or final cause
Divine presence 'in' things is constituted by immediate order and real coexistence of essence, not by spatial contact or intrinsic composition
God is in things by three general modes—essence, presence, power—grounded respectively in the divine essence, action, and power that concur in creation and conservation
Beyond the natural order, God is present in creatures by two further, more excellent modes proper to grace: hypostatic union and adoption
